Q: How to force Logstash to reparse a file? A:

Provide another configuration with

close_older => 1

The meaning of this configuration is to close the file after 1 second without any changes, and reopen it when there is new content. You can even set close_older => 0 to keep logstash closing and opening the file to obtain new content;

I encountered this problem in a window environment, where logstash cannot scroll through daily logs until the next day. With this configuration, it works. The official explanation for this configuration is as follows:


The file input closes any files that were last read the specified duration (seconds if a number is specified) ago. This has different implications depending on if a file is being tailed or read. If tailing, and there is a large time gap in incoming data the file can be closed (allowing other files to be opened) but will be queued for reopening when new data is detected. If reading, the file will be closed after closed_older seconds from when the last bytes were read. This setting is retained for backward compatibility if you upgrade the plugin to 4.1.0+, are reading not tailing and do not switch to using Read mode.

Q: Is there an official API or SDK to integrate Sham Cash with a Flutter mobile app? A:

To integrate ShamCash payments with Flutter, you need to find their merchant API or SDK, but currently, there isn't an official, public one documented for third-party apps, so users often rely on deep linking or redirect flows.

Q: asio: asio::awaitable<void> yield execution to other ready tasks A:

You can use asio::defer like:

co_await asio::defer(asio::use_awaitable);

or since asio 1.31 / boost 1.86 (co_await works with the more lightweight asio::deferred):

co_await asio::defer(asio::deferred);

or since asio 1.37 / boost 1.90 (asio::deferred becomes the default for asio::defer):

co_await asio::defer();

(live example on godbolt compiler explorer)

Why does this work?

The OPs "hack" with steady timer does schedule a completion handler to be run after the timer expires (which is immediately in this case).

The asio::defer function is a primitive, that directly schedules a completion handler to be run as soon as possible.

As both functions hook into the asio::async_result machinery, they both can be used with the asio::use_awaitable token that does the magic of creating a completion handler which resumes the coroutine if called.

Q: Compiler barrier for X86 lock prefixed instruction A:

Correct, GNU C Extended asm statements are purely a blackbox described by the constraints; changes to the template string have no effect on the optimizer.

The same statement without a "memory" clobber is how you'd implement a relaxed RMW, allowing compile-time reordering. (But of course this is x86; the runtime strength is still a full barrier, even stronger than as seq_cst operation needs to be.)

(Recent GCC (but not clang) gives Basic asm statements (no constraints) an implicit "memory" clobber for non-empty asm strings, going beyond the documented behaviour to help bad old code with things like asm("cli") be less broken. But Basic asm is always a bad idea except in naked functions (where it's the only valid option) and at global scope. )

GCC only processes the template string with string substitution, like a printf format string, after having already chosen where to put the operands based on the constraints. It emits that text as part of the asm output which gets fed to the assembler. (Clang by default uses its built-in assembler, so will also complain about asm syntax errors at compile time, since it doesn't have a separate assemble step unless you ask it to. But in terms of whether the template contents imply constraints, no, they don't.)

Fun fact: a "cc" clobber is implicit for i386 and amd64, so you don't have the option of leaving it out.

Fun fact #2: a "memory" clobber doesn't prevent reordering with local variables whose address hasn't escaped the function and aren't inputs to the asm statement. This is normally fine, and allows keeping loop counters in registers while the loop body has a "memory" clobber. The optimizer is constrained by a "memory" clobber the same way it would be by a non-inline function call with the same inputs as the asm statement, having to sync variable values with their memory storage if they're potentially globally reachable or via the operands. And of course has to assume that any/all such objects have been modified.

  • The difference between asm, asm volatile and clobbering memory
  • Why can `asm volatile("" ::: "memory")` serve as a compiler barrier?
  • Understanding volatile asm vs volatile variable
  • https://stackoverflow.com/tags/inline-assembly/info
  • https://gcc.gnu.org/wiki/DontUseInlineAsm

BTW, https://gcc.gnu.org/wiki/DontUseInlineAsm - in most code you should use either C11 stdatomic functions, or the GNU C __atomic builtins they're built in top of. For example if you want the ability to do atomic RMWs on variables that aren't _Atomic so can also be accessed efficiently when you know there are no concurrent accesses, like you can do with C++20 std::atomic_ref. Of course make sure you've aligned your variable sufficiently for it to be atomic, e.g. with _Alignas( sizeof(T) ) T foo; for types like int64_t or double on 32-bit targets like i386 where SysV ABI only gives them 4-byte alignment by default. (GCC will normally aim to give them natural alignment in 32-bit code, but the ABI's struct-packing rules can prevent that.)

T oldval = __atomic_fetch_add(p, val, __ATOMIC_ACQUIRE);
  // or __ATOMIC_SEQ_CST for example

This uses the C11 memory model like stdatomic, so is compatible with that. In practice it's also compatible with hand-rolled stuff using volatile and inline asm.
